planting.note: Plant bulb divisions in fall in moist, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; fly poison is the sole species in its genus and tolerates a wider range of soil textures and moisture than most of its Melanthiaceae relatives.

directions: Amianthium muscitoxicum is a monotypic native bulb of eastern North American woodlands, bogs, savannas, and sandy meadows, producing a low evergreen rosette of glossy, strap-like basal leaves and, in late spring, a stout leafless scape bearing a dense, oval cluster of small creamy-white flowers that age to green and then purplish-green as the capsules mature, giving the plant a long season of changing ornamental interest. It thrives in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to a few hours of direct sun and adapts to sand, loam, or clay so long as moisture is consistent, making it more forgiving than the strict bog or fen specialists in its family. The bulb, leaves, and seeds are all highly toxic to people and livestock if ingested, historically used to poison flies mixed with sugar and to kill crows raiding cornfields; plant well away from grazing animals and small children and handle bulbs with gloves. Slow to establish from seed but long-lived and reliable once settled, it is an excellent, low-maintenance accent for naturalized woodland edges and native meadow plantings.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in humus-rich, circumneutral to calcareous soil in shade; unlike its wetland relatives, Wood's false hellebore is a dry-mesic forest plant of undisturbed, often mafic or limestone-influenced slopes and does not want constant wet feet.

directions: Veratrum woodii is a rare and highly localized native perennial of mesic hardwood forests scattered from Ohio, Indiana, and Iowa south through Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, and Oklahoma to isolated Appalachian outliers, most often found on north- or east-facing lower slopes over mafic or calcareous bedrock in old, undisturbed woods. It forms a basal rosette of broad, pleated, corn-lily-like leaves from a large bulb, sending up a flowering stem to about 5 feet in mid-to-late summer topped with a loose panicle of small, distinctive maroon-purple to blackish-brown flowers that age to a dark purplish green, quite unlike the white or greenish-yellow blooms of its eastern and western cousins. Unlike Veratrum viride and V. californicum, it grows on drier, circumneutral to mildly alkaline soils rather than wet seeps and bogs, and it is notoriously slow to flower and set seed in the wild, so nursery-propagated divisions from reputable native plant specialists are strongly preferred over seed. All parts are highly toxic if ingested; handle bulbs and foliage with gloves and site away from livestock, pets, and children.
scientific_name_note: Also treated as Melanthium woodii in some modern regional floras (e.g., Flora of the Southeastern United States); listed here under the more widely used Veratrum woodii.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; mountain bunchflower is a higher-elevation Appalachian species found on mesic to dry-mesic oak-dominated slopes and mountain crests, so it tolerates drier footing than its wet-meadow relative M. virginicum.

directions: Melanthium parviflorum (mountain bunchflower) grows on mesic to dry-mesic, mixed-oak mountain slopes and crests at middle to high elevations through the central and southern Appalachians from Virginia to Alabama, a notably drier and higher-elevation habitat than its lowland relative Virginia bunchflower (M. virginicum). It forms a clump of long, strap-like basal leaves topped in summer by a loosely branched, open flowering stem bearing fewer and smaller flowers than its relatives, but with a striking bright emerald-green color and a distinctly musky, faintly marine scent that draws carrion-seeking pollinators. Reaching roughly 3 to 4.5 feet tall, it is a slower-spreading, more refined presence than the bolder M. virginicum and M. latifolium, and suits a shaded to partially shaded native rock garden or montane woodland planting with reliably drained, humus-rich soil. As with all Melanthium species, the foliage, flowers, and rhizomes are toxic if ingested; wear gloves when dividing.
scientific_name_note: Also known as Veratrum parviflorum in older floras; recent molecular studies support placement in Melanthium.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
Digital Atlas of the Virginia Flora

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; western featherbells naturally grows on wet cliffs, seepy banks, and moist mountain meadows and does not tolerate summer drought.

directions: Stenanthium occidentale is a diminutive native perennial of wet cliffs, seepy banks, and moist subalpine meadows and forests from British Columbia south through the Cascades and Rockies to northern California and western Montana, forming a small tuft of narrow, grass-like leaves from a slender bulb. In summer it sends up a short stem bearing an airy, one-sided raceme of small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers in shades of green, purple, and brown, giving it a much daintier and more pendulous habit than the upright, plume-like flower spikes of its eastern relatives S. gramineum and S. densum. It requires reliably moist to wet, cool soil year-round and is best suited to a shaded rock garden seep, streamside planting, or trough garden where its constant moisture needs can be met. Like other members of the bunchflower family, all parts are considered toxic if ingested.
